followUps:
It comes from semantic analysis, after parsing has already succeeded. The parser only checks grammar, and foo.bar() is grammatically fine whether or not foo exists.

The compiler then walks the AST with a symbol table (scopes mapping names to declarations). When it looks up count and finds no entry in any enclosing scope, it reports "cannot find symbol". A typo such as conut fails here, while a missing semicolon fails earlier, in the parser.

javac does very little optimisation; the JIT does almost all of it. javac mainly does constant folding (2 * 3 becomes 6), string-constant concatenation and desugaring (lambdas, enhanced for, generics erasure).

It cannot inline across classes or remove dead branches that depend on run-time facts, because classes can be loaded later. The JIT sees the real hot paths and types, so it does inlining, escape analysis, loop unrolling and devirtualisation. Keeping bytecode simple also helps the JIT recognise patterns.

Both: Java is compiled to bytecode by javac, and then the JVM interprets and JIT-compiles that bytecode at run time.

So the label depends on the stage. Source to bytecode is ahead-of-time compilation; bytecode to machine code is done by the interpreter at first, then by the C1 and C2 JIT compilers for methods called thousands of times. GraalVM native-image can also compile Java fully ahead of time into one executable.

Because a JIT compiles with facts that only exist at run time, while AOT code must be safe for every possible input.

Example: a virtual call shape.area() that has only ever seen Circle can be inlined behind a cheap class check, and then constant-folded. It also knows the exact CPU (AVX-512 or not) and the real branch frequencies. If an assumption breaks, it deoptimises. The cost is warm-up time and extra memory for the compiler.

code.title: AST versus parse tree: same expression, two trees

followUps:
Linters parse your file into an AST and then walk it, running small rules on the node types they care about.

An ESLint rule is a visitor: for example no-eval subscribes to CallExpression nodes and reports any whose callee is the identifier eval. Because it checks structure rather than text, it ignores "eval(x)" inside a string or comment. Rules can also use scope analysis and many provide auto-fixes by rewriting the tokens at a node's range.

Tree-sitter is an incremental parser generator used by editors for fast, error-tolerant syntax trees.

It builds a concrete syntax tree for a file in any supported language, and when you type one character it re-parses only the changed region, typically in milliseconds. Because it recovers from errors, the tree still exists while the code is half-written. Editors use it for syntax highlighting, code folding, structural selection and code search queries.

code.title: Recursive-descent calculator with precedence

followUps:
Add a level above multiplication that is called with right recursion instead of a loop, so 2 ^ 3 ^ 2 means 2 ^ (3 ^ 2) = 512, not 64.

Grammar: power -> atom ('^' power)?, and term now calls power instead of factor. Since power calls itself for the right side, the rightmost operator binds first. In a Pratt parser the same effect comes from giving the right binding power a lower value than the left.

double power() {
  double base = atom();
  if (peek() == '^') { pos++; return Math.pow(base, power()); }
  return base;
}

Add an identifier token, an environment map, and an assignment rule at the lowest precedence.

  1. Lexer: letters become IDENT tokens.
  2. factor: an IDENT looks its value up in a Map<String,Double>; unknown names raise an error.
  3. New top rule stmt -> IDENT '=' expr | expr; peek two tokens to see if an = follows the name.

Example: x = 3 + 4 stores 7, then x * 2 gives 14. Assignment is right-associative, so a = b = 1 works.

code.title: Strong dynamic typing in Python
code.python:
# Static/dynamic and strong/weak are separate axes. Python: dynamic + strong.
def show(label, fn):
    try:
        print(label, "->", repr(fn()))
    except Exception as e:
        print(label, "->", type(e).__name__ + ":", e)

x = 5
show('"5" + 2', lambda: "5" + 2)          # strong: no silent conversion
show('"5" * 2', lambda: "5" * 2)          # legal, but means repetition
show('int("5") + 2', lambda: int("5") + 2)  # explicit conversion works

# Dynamic: the type belongs to the value, so a name can be rebound to any type
x = "now a string"
print("x is now", type(x).__name__)

# Type hints are not enforced at run time (gradual typing)
def double(n: int) -> int:
    return n * 2
show("double(3)", lambda: double(3))
show('double("ab")', lambda: double("ab"))   # hint violated, nothing stops it
# A static checker (mypy) would reject the last call before running;
# the runtime only fails when an operation really cannot work.
show("double(None)", lambda: double(None))

followUps:
Static versus dynamic is about when types are checked; strong versus weak is about how freely values are silently converted. TypeScript is static, and Python is dynamic.

Python is also strong, because "5" + 2 raises TypeError while JavaScript quietly gives "52". TypeScript is not sound: any, type assertions (x as Foo), unchecked array indexing and bivariant method parameters let wrong types through. It was designed to be useful, not airtight. Data from the network is also never checked unless you validate it.

Inference lets the compiler work out the type itself from the right-hand side, so you do not write it, but the variable is still fully statically typed.

var n = 10; in Java is exactly int n = 10;, and later n = "hi" is a compile error. Rust goes further: let v = Vec::new(); gets its element type from a later v.push(3u8), using unification across the function. It is not dynamic typing, and the type is fixed at compile time.

Phi functions are placed at the iterated dominance frontier of each variable's assignments, which is the standard efficient method (Cytron et al.).

  1. Compute the dominator tree of the control-flow graph.
  2. Compute each block's dominance frontier: blocks where its dominance ends, i.e. merge points reachable from it.
  3. For each variable, put a phi at the frontier of every block that assigns it, repeating for the new phis until nothing changes.
  4. Rename variables by walking the dominator tree.

This avoids a phi at every merge for every variable, which would be quadratic.

Because SSA interference graphs are chordal, which means they can be coloured optimally in linear time, with no spilling guesswork.

In SSA each value is defined once and is live over a region dominated by its definition. The number of registers needed equals the maximum number of values live at one point (max-live). So you can first spill until max-live is at most K registers, then assign colours in dominance order and it always succeeds. Phi copies are resolved afterwards.

code.title: Why float sums cannot be reordered
code.python:
# Floating point is not associative, so a compiler may not reorder a sum
# unless told to (fast-math). Integers are exactly associative.
a, b, c = 1e16, -1e16, 1.0

left = (a + b) + c      # 0.0 + 1.0 = 1.0
right = a + (b + c)     # b + c rounds back to -1e16, then a + b = 0.0
print("a, b, c =", a, b, c)
print("(a + b) + c =", left)
print("a + (b + c) =", right)
print("same result?", left == right)

# Summing 0.1 ten times in different orders
vals = [0.1] * 10
fwd = 0.0
for v in vals: fwd += v
half = sum(vals[:5]) + sum(vals[5:])
print("forward sum  =", repr(fwd))
print("split sum    =", repr(half))

# Integers: any order gives the same answer, so reordering is legal
ints = [10**16, -10**16, 1]
print("int sums:", (ints[0] + ints[1]) + ints[2], ints[0] + (ints[1] + ints[2]))
# Lesson: an optimiser may only reorder what keeps observable results identical.

followUps:
Because the loop body usually has no observable effect, so the optimiser deletes it, and you are timing an empty loop.

If the result of for (i...) sum += i*i is never used, dead code elimination removes it, or constant folding replaces it with a closed-form value. The fix is to use the result: print it, return it, or sink it into a blackhole (JMH's Blackhole.consume). Also warm up the JIT, otherwise you measure the interpreter.

Because it removes the call overhead and, more importantly, it exposes the callee's body to every other optimisation in the caller.

After inlining square(x) into a loop, the compiler can see that x is constant, fold the arithmetic, hoist invariants, eliminate a null check, or avoid allocating the returned object via escape analysis. A call is an opaque barrier, and without inlining none of that is possible. The cost is larger code, which can overflow the instruction cache, so compilers inline hot and small methods first.

code.title: Tiny stack-based bytecode VM
code.python:
# A tiny stack-based bytecode VM: fetch - decode - execute loop.
# Program computes sum of 1..5 using a loop.
PUSH, LOAD, STORE, ADD, SUB, JNZ, PRINT, HALT = range(8)
NAMES = ["PUSH", "LOAD", "STORE", "ADD", "SUB", "JNZ", "PRINT", "HALT"]

code = [
    (PUSH, 0), (STORE, 0),     # total = 0
    (PUSH, 5), (STORE, 1),     # i = 5
    (LOAD, 0), (LOAD, 1), (ADD,), (STORE, 0),   # total += i   (pc 4)
    (LOAD, 1), (PUSH, 1), (SUB,), (STORE, 1),   # i -= 1
    (LOAD, 1), (JNZ, 4),       # if i != 0 goto 4
    (LOAD, 0), (PRINT,), (HALT,),
]

def run(code):
    stack, local, pc, steps = [], [0, 0], 0, 0   # operand stack, locals, program counter
    while True:
        ins = code[pc]                 # fetch
        op = ins[0]                    # decode
        pc += 1
        steps += 1
        if op == PUSH:   stack.append(ins[1])          # execute
        elif op == LOAD:  stack.append(local[ins[1]])
        elif op == STORE: local[ins[1]] = stack.pop()
        elif op == ADD:   b = stack.pop(); stack.append(stack.pop() + b)
        elif op == SUB:   b = stack.pop(); stack.append(stack.pop() - b)
        elif op == JNZ:
            if stack.pop() != 0: pc = ins[1]
        elif op == PRINT: print("output:", stack.pop())
        elif op == HALT:  return steps

print("program:", " ".join(NAMES[i[0]] for i in code))
n = run(code)
print("instructions dispatched:", n)   # each one pays a dispatch cost
# Cost: O(steps); a JIT would compile the loop and remove the dispatch.

followUps:
I would choose a stack VM first, and move to registers only if profiling shows dispatch is the bottleneck.

Stack code is simpler to generate (no register allocator, just post-order walk of the AST) and bytecode is compact: a+b is LOAD a, LOAD b, ADD. Register VMs (Lua 5.x, Dalvik) use noticeably fewer instructions, so fewer dispatches, but each instruction is wider and the compiler is harder. Pick by team time and measured speed, not by theory.

It runs a data-flow analysis over the bytecode that simulates the operand stack using types instead of values, and rejects the class if any path breaks the rules.

For every instruction it records the stack shape before it. At branches and merge points the shapes must agree, e.g. both paths arrive with [int, ref]. iadd needs two ints on top, so an empty stack is an underflow and a verification error. It iterates until the result stops changing. Modern class files carry StackMapTable hints so this takes one linear pass.

An inline cache remembers, at one call or property site, what it saw last time, so the next lookup is a single check instead of a full search.

At obj.x the site stores the object's shape and the offset of x. If the next object has the same shape, it reads that offset directly. One shape is monomorphic (fast), 2 to 4 is polymorphic (a short chain of checks), and more than that is megamorphic: it falls back to a slow generic hash lookup and usually cannot be inlined.

On-stack replacement (OSR) swaps a running method from interpreted code to compiled code in the middle of a loop, without waiting for the method to return.

Without it, a main that runs one loop of 10 million iterations would never reach the JIT, since it is only called once. When a loop's back-edge counter gets hot, the VM compiles a version entered at the loop header, copies the live locals from the interpreter frame into it, and jumps in. Deoptimisation is OSR in reverse.

Reference counting is fast and predictable but cannot free cycles, so CPython added a tracing cycle collector as a backup.

Refcounts free most objects instantly: when x = [1] goes out of scope, the list dies at once. But if a.other = b and b.other = a, both counts stay at 1 forever after you drop them. The gc module finds such unreachable groups periodically using generations (0, 1, 2) and frees them. Together you get prompt freeing in common cases.

Make one side of the relationship weak (or unowned when the target always outlives it), so it does not add to the count.

Classic case: a view controller owns a closure, and the closure captures self strongly, giving 2 objects with count 1 each that never free. Write [weak self] in and use guard let self else { return }. Parent to child is strong, child to parent is weak. Find the leak with Xcode's Memory Graph, which shows the cycle.

code.title: Mark-sweep fragmentation and compaction
code.python:
# Mark-sweep leaves holes; mark-compact slides live objects together.
# Heap = list of 12 cells; each object is (name, size, start).
heap_size = 12
objs = {"A": [2, 0], "B": [3, 2], "C": [1, 5], "D": [4, 6], "E": [2, 10]}  # size, start
refs = {"A": [], "C": [], "B": [], "D": ["E"], "E": []}
roots = ["B", "D"]                       # A and C are garbage

def mark():
    live, todo = set(), list(roots)
    while todo:                          # DFS from the roots: O(live)
        o = todo.pop()
        if o not in live:
            live.add(o); todo += refs[o]
    return live

def draw(label):
    cells = ["."] * heap_size
    for n, (size, start) in objs.items():
        for i in range(start, start + size): cells[i] = n
    print(label.ljust(14), "".join(cells))

def biggest_hole():
    cells = [True] * heap_size
    for size, start in objs.values():
        for i in range(start, start + size): cells[i] = False
    best = run = 0
    for free in cells:
        run = run + 1 if free else 0
        best = max(best, run)
    return best

draw("before GC:")
live = mark()
print("marked live:", sorted(live))
for n in list(objs):                     # sweep: O(heap)
    if n not in live: del objs[n]
draw("after sweep:")
print("largest free block:", biggest_hole(), "(free total 3, a 3-cell request fails)")

pos = 0
for n in sorted(objs, key=lambda k: objs[k][1]):   # compact: slide left
    objs[n][1] = pos; pos += objs[n][0]
draw("after compact:")
print("largest free block:", biggest_hole())

followUps:
GC roots are the starting points the collector treats as definitely alive: everything reachable from them is kept.

In the JVM they are local variables and parameters on each thread's stack, static fields of loaded classes, JNI global references, active threads, and objects held by the monitor or class loader internals. Example: a static Map cache is a root, so every entry stays alive until you remove it. That is why unbounded static caches cause leaks.

Because moving large objects is expensive, so by default the LOH is swept and its free space reused but not compacted.

Objects of 85,000 bytes or more go to the LOH. Copying a 100 MB array and fixing every reference to it costs more than the fragmentation usually hurts. If fragmentation causes out-of-memory errors you can set GCSettings.LargeObjectHeapCompactionMode = CompactOnce for the next blocking GC, or pool large buffers with ArrayPool instead of allocating them.

Objects that should have died young get promoted to the old generation, where they fill it up and trigger slow full collections.

Example: a request handler allocates 50 MB of temporary objects per second, but the young gen is only 20 MB, so a minor GC fires while many are still in use and they survive and are promoted. The old gen then grows and a full GC, with long pauses, follows. Fix by reducing allocation, enlarging the young gen, or raising the tenuring threshold, and watch the promotion rate in the GC log.

Go's collector is non-generational by design: it is concurrent mark-sweep, tuned for low pause times rather than for copying young objects.

Go's escape analysis already puts many short-lived values on the stack, so fewer objects reach the heap. A generational collector would need a write barrier on every pointer store and to move objects, which conflicts with Go's interior pointers and non-moving heap. The team found the extra complexity was not worth it. Allocation is still cheap with per-thread caches.

The collector falls behind: either it makes the program wait (an allocation stall) or, if the heap runs out, it falls back to a full stop-the-world collection.

Concurrent collectors need free memory to allocate into while marking runs. If threads allocate faster than the collector reclaims, the headroom hits zero. ZGC then stalls allocating threads; G1 reports "to-space exhausted" and does a full GC; Go makes the allocating goroutine do mark assist work. The fix is a bigger heap, less allocation, or more GC threads.

Because moving objects concurrently is only safe if every read checks for a moved object, and a load barrier does that check exactly when a reference is read.

ZGC relocates live objects while the program runs. A stale pointer to the old copy could be read at any time, and a write barrier would not catch reads. The load barrier looks at the colour bits in the pointer; if they say "not yet remapped", it fixes the pointer to the new address and heals the field. The cost is a small check on each reference load.

Open the heap dump in a tool (Eclipse MAT or VisualVM) and look at which objects retain the most memory: the dominator tree sorts them by retained size.

Object A dominates B if every path from a GC root to B goes through A, so freeing A frees B. Sorting by retained size shows, for example, one HashMap holding 1.2 GB of a 1.5 GB heap. Expand it, see the entries, then use "path to GC roots" to find which static field or thread holds it. That is your leak.

Pick Parallel GC when you care about total throughput and not about individual pauses, such as batch jobs, data processing or tests.

Parallel stops the world and collects with all cores, which wastes the least CPU, with no barrier overhead on the application. A nightly 10-minute job that runs for 4 hours does not care about a 3-second pause. ZGC is better when a service has latency targets (p99 under 10 ms), but it uses more CPU and memory headroom. Measure both on your own workload.

Compile each rule once, key the result by a hash of its source text plus the language version, and reuse it.

Use a bounded LRU map hash(source + version) -> compiled program, so edits create a new key and old entries age out. Compiled programs must be immutable and stateless so many threads can run them at once; the per-run state (variables, fuel counter) lives in a fresh context. Compile at save time, so syntax errors reach the author and runtime only loads. A cache hit saves the parse, which is often 90% of the work for short rules.

Store the language version with every saved rule, and keep old versions working by migrating or by keeping an old interpreter path, never by silently changing meaning.

  • Add only: new functions and keywords are backwards compatible.
  • Breaking change: bump the version, keep the old behaviour for rules saved under it.
  • Write an automated migration for old rules, with golden tests from real saved rules replayed on each release.

Example: version 2 changes / from integer to decimal; v1 rules keep integer division.
